summary:
Brunei's Syariah Penal Code Order 2013 criminalises a man dressing as a woman or a woman dressing as a man "without reasonable excuse" or "for immoral purposes", an offence under Section 198(1). Human Rights Watch's survey of laws criminalising same-sex relations and gender expression identifies Brunei as one of at least two countries whose national law expressly penalises "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex. The provision is enforced. On 17 October 2014 religious law enforcers detained a 38-year-old unmarried Muslim civil servant at Bangunan Bumiputera in Bandar Seri Begawan, finding women's personal items in his bag; he pleaded guilty to cross-dressing in a public place and on 11 March 2015 was fined B$1,000 with 60 days' imprisonment in default.

The United States Department of State's 2017 human rights report recorded no known convictions under the cross-dressing ban that year and stated that morality provisions covering cross-dressing, alcohol, Ramadan eating and religious propagation were enforced, while the sharia implementing regulations remained unissued.

A trans visitor cannot align travel documents with presentation. Brunei does not permit a change of name or gender on official documents, and sex reassignment surgery is not permitted in the country.

Penalties for sexual conduct escalate sharply. Under the Syariah Penal Code Order the de jure penalty for sex between men is death by stoning where the parties are married and the evidentiary threshold is met, either by admission or by the testimony of four adult male Muslim eyewitnesses. Where that threshold is not met the maximum is seven years' imprisonment and thirty strokes of whipping, which is also the penalty applied while the death penalty moratorium continues. For unmarried men the penalty is one year in prison or 100 lashes. Sex between women carries any two of three penalties: forty lashes of caning, up to ten years' imprisonment, and a fine of up to B$40,000.

The third stage of the Syariah Penal Code Order took effect on 3 April 2019, introducing stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, and forty strokes of the cane for sex between women. The code applies principally to Muslims, roughly two-thirds of the population. Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957.

In May 2019 the government extended its moratorium on the death penalty to cover the Syariah Penal Code Order, so the stoning provisions are not carried out while the moratorium holds. The moratorium was still in effect as of May 2023 and was confirmed in force at a check on 27 September 2026. It is revocable at any time by the absolute monarch with minimal process and without warning.

Secular law also criminalises "carnal intercourse against the order of nature". A July amendment to Chapter 22 of the Penal Code Order raised the minimum sentence to between 20 and 50 years' imprisonment; it is applied primarily in cases of rape or child abuse where both the attacker and the victim are male.

Reporting from April 2019 recorded no assurance that the new provisions would not be enforced against foreigners, and anonymous accounts from Brunei described a climate of fear among the people affected.
tangentialFactors:
Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal in Brunei since 1906, under Straits Settlements law applied through the 1906 Courts Enactment as updated in 1908, and remained illegal after independence in 1984. Before the 2019 implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order, homosexual acts were punishable by up to ten years' imprisonment even when private and consensual.

Human Rights Watch's global survey counts at least 67 countries criminalising same-sex relations and at least nine criminalising gender expression. Brunei is one of at least two countries, alongside Oman, whose national law expressly criminalises "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex; a state-level sharia analogue exists in Malaysia.

The final stage of the code drew condemnation from the United Nations and from foreign governments, and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged Brunei to halt it. OutRight Action International has described Brunei as having the most worrisome state of rights for LGBT people in Southeast Asia.
localsOnly:
Police intimidation of LGBTI people in Brunei is documented, including threats to make a person's sexuality public in order to obstruct their obtaining a government job or to bar their graduation from government academic institutions. Members of the community reported that the government monitored their activities and communications.

Events on LGBTI topics are subject to restrictions on assembly and expression, with the government reportedly refusing permits for such events. LGBTI residents reported discrimination in public and private employment, housing, recreation, and in obtaining services including education from state entities. Bruneian society is described as associating homosexuality with "effeminate men".

No independent human rights organisations are active in Brunei. The Brunei Project has monitored human rights in the country since May 2015, with transgender and intersex rights among its concerns, and in May 2016 held Brunei's first International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia event with local activists and regional organisations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The text of Brunei's Penal Code, including the Syariah Penal Code provisions, could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), and a related academic paper on the sharia penal code was likewise unavailable (HTTP 403). The statutory wording cited here rests on secondary sources.

No entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to transgender travellers were located, and no sourced account was found of how immigration or security screening treats a trans visitor's documents or presentation.

The 2017 finding of no known convictions under the cross-dressing ban is a null result and does not establish that the provision goes unenforced. The claim that a person convicted of "tarnishing the image of Islam" may be heavily punished is recorded without citation to a provision or a stated penalty.

The duration of the death penalty moratorium is unresolved beyond the last confirmed check; the sources state only that it remains revocable without notice.
